speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the aftermath of the Global Financial Crisis, the Financial Stability Board (FSB), an international organisation comprising policymakers and financial regulators around the world, was established to promote international financial stability.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS, as a member of FSB has been actively involved in the development of its recommendations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The 2012 amendment also drew on our own review in light of Singapore's experience in the crisis and sought to strengthen safeguards for retail investors and enhance MAS' supervision and enforcement powers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As the amendments are wide-ranging, MAS had indicated then that the reforms to strengthen the regulation of OTC derivatives would be undertaken in two phases for effective implementation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The first phase of reforms undertaken in 2012 requires contract details of OTC derivatives transactions, such as the size, mark-to-market value and maturity, to be reported to licensed trade repositories.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This enables MAS to monitor any potential financial stability risks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Central clearing will mitigate the counterparty credit risks inherent in such trades and limit the effects of systemic contagion.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This Bill implements the remaining aspects of the reforms in OTC derivatives reforms and regulations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS also took the opportunity to amend the SFA in three other key areas: first, enhancing regulatory safeguards for retail investors; second, enhancing credibility and transparency of capital markets; and third, strengthening the enforcement regime against market misconduct.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS has consulted the industry and the public on the proposed amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It has considered all the feedback received and taken them into account as appropriate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will now go through the amendments in turn.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The events leading to the collapse of major financial institutions during the Global Financial Crisis exposed significant weaknesses in the structure of OTC derivatives markets, necessitating regulatory reforms.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a leading financial centre and an active member of FSB, it is important that we align to these latest international standards and best practices.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This Bill completes the reforms to further enhance transparency and improve supervisory oversight of our OTC derivatives market operators and intermediaries.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Internationally, the United States (US) and Japan have commenced their requirements to trade OTC derivatives products on organised trading facilities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Others, like the European Union, Hong Kong and Australia, have yet to do so, despite having the legal frameworks in place.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS will continue to monitor international developments and market liquidity conditions in determining the timing and scope of implementing the trading requirement in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Operators of organised trading facilities for OTC derivatives products will have to be authorised by MAS and must comply with requirements aimed at maintaining fair, orderly and transparent markets.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Intermediaries in the OTC derivatives markets will also be subject to regulation to ensure that risks associated with their activities are well-managed.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: While the Bill tightens the OTC derivatives regime to better safeguard financial stability, we also need to strike a balance against our objective to promote ease of doing business, innovation and a vibrant financial sector.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As part of this effort, this Bill therefore also seeks to streamline existing regulatory regimes for commodity derivatives and exchange-traded derivatives.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Commodity derivatives market operators and intermediaries, which are currently regulated under the Commodity Trading Act administered by International Enterprise (IE) Singapore, will consequently be regulated under SFA.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This avoids subjecting them to two regulatory regimes and ensures more efficient regulation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS will provide for appropriate transition periods to minimise any industry impact.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS will also allow derivatives products to be listed and traded on organised trading facilities without the need for case-by-case approval.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They will be required to certify that the contract design satisfies conditions required for fair, orderly and transparent trading.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As these conditions will be set out publicly, market operators will clearly know the boundaries within which they can design their products.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They will not need to seek MAS' approval.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The streamlined listing process will enable our market operators to innovate and launch new derivatives products to meet market demands.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Reducing the time-to-market could also encourage trading of derivatives contracts on organised trading facilities, instead of OTC, without MAS having to specifically require such products for platform trading.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A primary objective of MAS' regulatory framework for capital markets aims to safeguard the interests of retail investors, who are really the man-in-the-street, putting their savings and nest egg in investment products.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We want to ensure these investors have access to adequate information and that intermediaries deal fairly with them.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is why: First, public offers of securities, such as shares and bonds and investment funds, must be made with a prospectus registered with MAS.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The prospectus must contain all material information relating to the investment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, intermediaries, such as brokers, financial advisers and fund managers, must be licensed by MAS and adhere to rules governing their conduct of business with customers in a fair, transparent manner.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In recent years, MAS has observed a number of non-conventional products that are marketed to retail investors as alternate investments.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some of these products display essentially the same characteristics as traditional capital markets products but are deliberately structured to fall out of MAS' regulatory framework.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To enhance investor protection, the Bill provides MAS greater flexibility and powers to bring non-conventional investment products within MAS' regulatory perimeters.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, the Bill empowers MAS to prescribe certain products as debentures.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is because, in substance, such schemes are similar to collateralised borrowing arrangements.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Once classified as a debenture, offers of products with such buy-back arrangements will have to be made with a prospectus registered with MAS.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This will provide retail investors better access to information on product features and risks and make more informed investment decisions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, the Bill widens the definition of collective investment schemes (CIS), which must be authorised or recognised by MAS for public offers made available to retail investors.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But investment schemes can be structured to sell investors sub-divided interests in physical assets, such as undeveloped land, plantation plots or even units in an apartment block to be run as a hotel.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Such schemes have typically been called land-banking, plantation schemes, and condo-tels respectively.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: By structuring the schemes this way, the pooling element can be avoided, and regulation as a CIS circumvented.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A scheme can be caught as CIS as long as the scheme property is managed as a whole.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This recognises the "collective" nature of such schemes, since property is still managed as a whole by the scheme manager, to generate profits for the collective interests of scheme investors.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Such arrangements, in substance, pose the same risks to investors as traditional CIS, and should be regulated as such.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is the approach adopted in the United Kingdom and Hong Kong.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the same time, we do not want to extend the regulatory perimeter too far.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The amendment will not capture schemes which are predominantly for the consumption of, rather than investment in, property, or where property is managed for the benefit of investors on an individual basis.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, arrangements where property owners simply use the same operator to help them let out their individual apartment units, will not be considered as a CIS.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Investors need to critically assess investment products and refrain from investing in any product that they do not understand or where the returns sound too good to be true.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The next set of amendments relate to the classification of non-retail investors.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are two main types of non-retail investors under MAS' capital markets regulatory framework.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, accredited investors (AIs), who are identified based on prescribed wealth or income thresholds; and Two, institutional investors, who are widely accepted as having a high degree of financial knowledge.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Such investors are generally considered better able to protect their own interests, as compared to retail investors.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In line with a measured regulatory approach, there are available exemptions from regulatory requirements for those who deal only with non-retail investors.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Currently, individuals qualify as AIs if they have more than $2 million of net personal assets.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Bill also introduces another avenue for individuals to qualify as AIs if they have more than $1 million of financial assets, net of any related liabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With this amendment, individuals whose wealth is concentrated in their primary residence, with few other liquid assets to invest, will be treated as retail investors and will benefit from the range of regulatory safeguards under the SFA when transacting in capital markets products.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS also intends to introduce in subsidiary legislation an opt-in regime for the AI class.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, even if an investor qualifies as an AI, intermediaries cannot automatically treat him as such.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Instead, intermediaries will have to inform the investor of the trade-offs involved and get his agreement to be treated as an AI.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The investor can choose not to opt-in and remain as a retail investor with greater regulatory safeguards; or he may willingly forego such safeguards in order to more easily access a wider range of niche financial products and services, likely more complex and with higher risk.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The choice is ultimately his or hers to make, dependent on his or her own risk profile, investment needs and circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Bill also amends the institutional investor class to cover a wider range of entities that are professionally active in the capital markets.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These institutions are sophisticated in their investment approach and should, therefore, be accorded minimal safeguards.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This includes financial institutions that are regulated by a foreign regulator, foreign central governments and sovereign wealth funds.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: On the other hand, statutory bodies, other than prescribed Statutory Boards, such as the Central Provident Fund (CPF) Board or even MAS, will no longer be deemed as institutional investors.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many such entities, such as Town Councils and religious bodies, do not always possess the level of financial sophistication to be deemed an institutional investor.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But as explained above, they can opt-in as AIs if they meet the criteria, which, for corporations, include having $10 million or more in net assets.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These changes take into account global best practices recommended by the International Organisation of Securities Commission (IOSCO), the international standard-setting body for securities markets.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS is an active member of the Commission and has contributed to formulating best practices.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Financial benchmarks play an important role in the pricing and settlement of financial instruments and contracts.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One example is the Singapore Interbank Offer Rate (SIBOR), which is used by various lenders to set interest rates.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As it has wide systemic influence, it is critical that the process of setting financial benchmarks is credible and reliable.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Following the uncovering of misconduct in the setting of the London Interbank Offered Rate, IOSCO has developed principles to address vulnerabilities in the benchmark-setting process.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Regulatory frameworks for financial benchmarks have been implemented in the United Kingdom and are in the process of being implemented at the European level.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Once designated, MAS will regulate those who administer these benchmarks as well as those who submit the information required to compute these benchmarks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Both are widely referenced by banks to set interest rates for commercial term loans and residential property loans; it is thus important that the setting of these benchmarks be subject to a robust and credible process.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Bill also introduces criminal sanctions and civil penalties to deter manipulation of financial benchmarks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This will cover manipulative acts that occur in Singapore or are committed in relation to financial benchmarks administered in Singapore, even if the acts are perpetrated overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Next, we will strengthen disclosure requirements for short selling of listed securities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Short selling is the practice of selling securities that one does not own.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It enhances the price discovery process by allowing market participants who hold a negative view on the price of a security to express this view.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The efficacy of the price discovery process can be improved by making available to all market participants information on the extent of any such short selling in a security.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In line with jurisdictions, such as Australia, Europe and Hong Kong, the Bill introduces disclosure requirements on the level of short-sell orders and short positions in securities listed on an approved exchange in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Bill requires market participants to specifically indicate short-sell orders, giving statutory effect to reporting obligations currently imposed through the trading rules of the Singapore Exchange.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Those who hold outstanding short positions above a prescribed threshold will also be required to report those short positions to MAS.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Aggregated short-sell orders and short positions will be made available to the public, so that they can make more informed investment decisions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Section 199 of SFA currently prohibits disclosures of statements that are false or misleading in a material aspect and are likely to have an effect on the market price of securities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the 2012 case of Madhavan Peter vs Public Prosecutor, the Court held that a significant price effect is required for liability to be established against a person with respect to false or misleading statements under section 199.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Price movements of securities may be affected by other contemporaneous and irrelevant market factors, such as the general market sentiment or market liquidity.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As such, MAS' ability to take enforcement action against materially false or misleading disclosures that may wrongly influence persons to trade in the market should not be constrained by the requirement of a significant price effect.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Bill also introduces a statutory definition of "persons who commonly invest", to better reflect market participants who are accustomed to or likely to invest in securities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This term − which is currently not defined in SFA − will be used as the reference point in insider trading cases or assessing whether a particular information is generally available and is likely to have a material price impact by influencing the behaviour of common investors.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the 2012 case of Lew Chee Fai Kevin vs MAS on insider trading, the Court of Appeal held that "persons who commonly invest" are reasonable investors who possess general professional knowledge, but do not include retail investors who trade regularly.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Court also defined "general professional knowledge" as having a very high standard of market analysis and trading knowledge.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is not reflective of the average investor in the market.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Court will be able to take into account the reality that there can be different classes of "persons who commonly invest", each with a different level of knowledge and expertise.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS will issue guidelines on the interpretation of this statutory definition.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Currently, the maximum civil penalty that can be awarded against an individual is capped at three times the benefits gained or losses avoided, subject to a minimum of $50,000.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, where the benefits gained or losses avoided are small, the civil penalty is effectively $50,000 and may not adequately reflect the culpability of the offender or achieve sufficient deterrence.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: On the other hand, where there is no benefit gained or loss avoided, the civil penalty can be much higher, currently capped at $2 million.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This ensures that the civil penalty quantum that can be awarded is commensurate with the gravity of the misconduct and is not unduly limited by the value of the benefit gained or loss avoided by the offender.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Such priority will strengthen MAS' ability to resist attempts by third party creditors to divert funds frozen by MAS under the civil penalty regime towards satisfaction of the contravening person's private debts.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is in line with the priority that is accorded to Government claims in other civil proceedings taken by the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS will continue to review its capital markets regulatory framework to ensure that it keeps pace with market developments and international standards and supports the growth of Singapore's economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From real estate to insurance to banking and more, we offer local and global investors direct access to a plethora of regional and global investment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Economic and political stability, robustness of the legal and regulatory framework as well as the reliability and transparency in the way business is conducted also helped to enhance our reputation as a top wealth management and regional derivatives hub.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The vibrancy of the financial sector has led to a tremendous growth of the sector and we now have over 200 banks with a presence in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The growth of the local and global capital markets has created a lot of wealth in the past decades and this has also given rise to the notion that it may be easy to make money from investments and that the risk of failure is low.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It may not be uncommon for beginners to jump into hefty investments based on blind trust for a friend or financial consultant.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is especially important as investment products have gone beyond plain vanilla to highly complex structures.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Investor protection in Singapore is pertinent, given Singapore's standing as a pre-eminent global financial centre, its value-added growth contributions to the Singapore economy and its role as an intermediary for various players in the economy is also important.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is the responsibility and moral obligation of financial institutions to explain to their clients, especially those who are investing in complex instruments, and ensure that risks are properly understood before making an investment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The market operates like the car windscreen wiper, if I can make an analogy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It can swing to the left and also to the right.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, you can lose money in as much as you can make it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In fact, in certain cases where the clients use leverage, they may even lose more than their initial capital.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Bond investors are often lured with coupons or better interest rates without being explained that higher rates mean higher risk of loss as the quality of the underlying instrument is often poorer.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Retail investors may feel that because the persons selling investment products are from the financial industry, they would have better knowledge of the market and are trustworthy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What they fail to appreciate is that these same people are selling the products also because they have to meet their targets and their key performance indicators.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Conflicts of interests may also not be properly disclosed to investors and this may prevent investors from making informed decisions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A retail investor may be told not to worry about the corporation issuing the bond because their parent company is a big company with a good track record.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What investors do not understand is that the bond may not be issued by the parent company but a subsidiary which is a separate corporate entity altogether and which may have limited assets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another point is the investors may be told that the bond may have this and that rating from one of the bond rating agencies, for example, Fitch, Moody's or Standard and Poor's.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But many of them may not actually understand or are able to truly explain what these ratings mean.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In today's market, we must remember the phrase: "nothing is too big to fail".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another bug-bear is the use of financial jargons which may impress the retail investor that you are someone knowledgeable but, at the same time, confuse the investor.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The investors may find themselves persuaded into buying products when the risks are not fully explained.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Look at how the fall in oil prices impacted on the oil and gas industry, resulting in a series of bond defaults.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Disclaimer clauses and additional contractual obligations, often neglected or discretely mentioned amidst a wall of incomprehensible financial terms, may be skimmed over and never explained.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have seen how some of our residents who face losses investing in some of these schemes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In fact, if I may suggest, MAS should perhaps not allow the primary residence of the investor to be used to contribute to the net personal assets to meet the S$2 million threshold.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A family can one day find themselves having to sell their home if they are not careful in investing on the basis of using their primary residence to pledge against any open positions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Additionally, in light of inflation, a higher threshold than S$2 million net worth should be established.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the US, although the qualifying net worth is US$1 million for an individual to be an AI, levels of consumer protection are higher due to the fact that litigation and regulatory activism are prolific in the US.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: By contrast, in Singapore, this is not in our culture.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Regardless, wealth should not be the sole major indicator here, as being rich in asset does not necessarily mean good financial knowledge.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To better increase protection, the threshold for attaining Approved Investor status should be raised based on his or her experience and expertise.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I hope the Government will consider placing greater emphasis on the importance of knowledge in investing, rather than just personal assets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We can create any number of laws and restrictions but, ultimately, nothing empowers a customer more than possessing knowledge.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, I would like to point out some potential gaps.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the case of joint accounts, when one party is a non-AI, he or she can opt out of protection measures available to retail investors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While it may be common in the wealth management industry where only one joint account holder is an AI, for example, a millionaire father with a joint banking account with his son who is still in university, we cannot over regulate to not permit non-AIs from being joint account holders.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It may be prudent to add a requirement that mandates banks to primarily deal with the party who is the AI, if the investment products sold are not permitted to be sold to retail investors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Additionally, for accounts opened in the name of a private investment company or trust, where there is more than one beneficial owner, all beneficial owners need to qualify as an accredited investor.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This may not be reflective of how potential private banking clients operate their accounts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is proposed that the laws should be revised to ensure consistency so that beneficial owners of such structures, such as trust or private investment company accounts who may not be AIs are placed on the same footing as those who choose to invest as joint account holders.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is almost always to the bank's benefit to deal with AIs over retail investors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My concern is that some bankers may not be properly incentivised to accurately determine a customer's net assets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, a careless banker may "overestimate" a potential client's net assets so as to "upgrade" him to an AI.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Lessons from the recent 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB) money laundering scandal should be a stark reminder that self-regulation by banks may not be completely effective in some areas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, having a third party to do the assessment may be fairer and more transparent.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a global financial centre with many non-Singaporean clients, in order to uphold our good reputation, the Government has a duty to look out for the interests of our overseas investors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, it is important to make clear that all protection for local investors should apply to all overseas investors as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Conversely, the interests of Singaporeans must also not be neglected in a bid to cater to the foreign financial entities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Last, but not least, the timing and implementation period of the changes in the Securities and Futures Bill would be critical.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the potential of some level of deregulation coming out of the US under the Trump administration, it may be essential to communicate the main broad objectives of this amendment to the public and financial institutions, as it signals a move towards slightly tighter regulation which can be interpreted as onerous.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Overall, the changes, particularly its elements of investor protection, including that for commodity-related products, as well as enforcement action, are highly lauded and should ensure a more resilient, transparent and stable financial sector.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the whole, these changes are positive and, in fact, overdue.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While I do not oppose the Bill, I would like to seek clarifications on some aspects of the Bill and make some comments on gaps that remain unaddressed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must be seen to be progressive and advanced, taking into consideration global best practices and leading edge developments in technology and business models.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is, of course, necessary to attract investments and create jobs in our financial services industry.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is also necessary to broaden investment options for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the same time, our ecosystem must be seen to be fair and transparent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should never allow it to be seen as a rigged game, which insiders can exploit for unfair advantages over the smaller players or retail investors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To allow this, is to risk weakening the viability of our financial services industry and, indeed, our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have seen in other countries how there can be a public backlash against traders and market-movers who can make personal incomes of up to $100 million a year or more, seemingly, by not creating anything of value to society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, we need to get the balance right.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Too much regulation, and we risk strangling business, investment job creation and wealth creation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Too little regulation, and we risk feeding the perception that the markets are a rigged game.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Complex regulations are only as good as the regulator's ability to enforce those regulations, lest they become, in Shakespeare's words, "rules more honoured in the breach than the observance".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Insider trading is a good example of this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Insider trading crimes are difficult to prove in Court and require strong expertise and capabilities on the part of investigators and prosecutors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, no regulator and no policing regime can be perfect, but what measures are being put in place to ensure a reasonably robust regime for detecting possible breaches, investigating them and, where warranted, bringing them to the Courts?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It took several years for the authorities to bring charges, in the case of the penny stocks saga.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This episode, which saw share prices see-saw, has unnerved retail investors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In my grassroots work, I met a retired resident who lived in a 3-room flat, who had invested small amounts of his money in the local stock market.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, numbers were not cited for the level of investment that we put into enforcement, either in terms of budget or staffing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Specifically, I would like to ask a few questions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is this ratio commensurate with what we see in other enforcement agencies, like the British Serious Fraud Office or the American Securities and Exchange Commission, for instance?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reason I ask this is that good systems for generating intelligence will be useless if the staff who have to sieve through the data are overwhelmed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, on this subject, I would like to pose a question about the robustness of our enforcement regime that is broader.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And specifically, are there rules in place to control the ease with which Government employees with financial industry oversight responsibilities can join financial institutions immediately after they leave Government service?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are there rules in place which require such employees to exercise a cooling-off period, before they can join industries that they used to help regulate?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In other countries, this matter has been a subject of some debate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The concern fuelling such debates is easy to see.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If a tendency takes root whereby regulators often leave their Civil Service jobs to take up positions in the industries they used to regulate, sometimes with the expressed responsibility to manage communications with the Government, there is the possibility that serving regulators may be at risk of industry capture.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What this means is that the regulators may tend to keep one eye on the interests of the industry that they are regulating, knowing that they may one day, sooner or later, join the employer of that industry.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example – and this example does not relate to the financial services industry or indeed to regulation per se, but the principle is the same – on 9 December 2016, US President-elect Donald Trump floated the idea that US military procurement officials should be banned for life from ever joining defence contractors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I would like to query the changes made to the definition of an AI.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The aim of this change seems to be to ensure that AIs have at least S$1 million in liquid assets, that is, financial assets net of the property they reside in, which is a reasonable intent, and one that I agree with.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By virtue of total premiums paid, maturity value of the policy or some other criteria?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the moment, some banks depend on investors' self-declaration in form filling.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will financial service institutions (FSIs) be required to ascertain mark-to-market prices for the properties and financial assets that the investors declare?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, this may saddle FSIs with higher compliance costs, costs which may get passed on to their customers to some extent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But in any case, it would be important and useful for the position to be clarified so that FSIs are held to the same standard and are consistent in their practices.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are illiquid bonds included in the definition of "financial assets" or should we differentiate between illiquid and liquid bonds to be considered within the S$1 million financial asset threshold?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As these questions demonstrate, it may be necessary for MAS to be more prescriptive about how these legislative changes to the definition of an AI will, in practice, be operationalised.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Speaker, I support the Securities and Futures (Amendment) Bill, mainly for two reasons.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Recently, I read a newspaper article in Lianhe Wanbao, and the headline is, "Sleepless Nights for elderly couple who lose $30,000".

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: An elderly retired couple attended an investment talk and forked out $10,000 to buy bonds.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The other party promised they would get back their principal plus 10% interest within a year.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, when the bond matured, they did not get their principal back.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This elderly couple has been suffering from insomnia because they would also lose their further investment of $20,000 in bonds which are about to mature.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This is by no means an isolated case, as there are many other similar stories.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: There are so many types of financial products in the market now and many seniors hope to retire comfortably using these avenues of wealth management, but not all investors are savvy enough or equipped with the necessary knowledge to evaluate the risks and the merits of a financial product.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The sales executives tend to be glib and persuasive and those with no investment experience can be easily misled.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Based on the current legislation, investors' risk category is defined according to their financial assets, including the value of their properties.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, some investors may have financial assets of $2 million, but this is mainly in property, with very little in cash.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Once the investment fails, practically everything is wiped out, bringing their quality of life under jeopardy.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The second reason is that the amendment of the Bill would widen the scope of governance and ensure that transactions are properly regulated.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In recent years, some "non-conventional investment products" have become increasingly popular, like precious metals, red wine, land banking and so on.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Prior to the amendment, with the exception of collective investments, these non-conventional investment products do not come under the purview of MAS.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In order to avoid coming under MAS regulation, some market players have become very creative and restructured their products.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, besides these two points, I still have some reservations.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Overly strict controls may make the financial markets stagnate.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: A prosperous and lively market has to have some element of risk.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: How could the Government achieve a balance between the two?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: For example, small and medium enterprises (SMEs) always encounter problems of financing.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: There is a new financing method called crowdfunding, which could provide capital for SMEs and startup companies.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: After amending the Securities and Futures Act, this could hamper such new funding channels.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I hope that when the Government decides to stipulate related legislation in the future, it could strike a balance between maintaining an active market and strengthening governance.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: An over-regulated system could produce the "hairy-crab effect" of constraining the markets.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The desire to achieve a balance between financial innovation and effective governance is a tall order and a real test of management wisdom.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, I would like to seek a few clarifications.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today, a retail investor can access and trade various financial products, such as stocks, bonds, futures and options, through voice or electronic trading.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, this ease of access and the wide range of financial products could bring about unintended consequences, especially for retail investors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The complexities of such derivative products may not be fully understood by a retail investor who lacks access to professional advisory services.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While an investor with the privilege of a private banker's advisory may be well-hedged against such risks, I remain concerned for retail investors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We must always strengthen our regulatory framework to ensure the average retail investor is protected, as they remain exposed to an increasing range of investible products, in particular, financial derivatives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Asymmetrical information generally contributes to false triggers and leads to costly investment decisions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, educating retail investors should and must always remain a key focus of financial market regulation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share how the Ministry intends to do this?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Most importantly, it would deter excessive short selling by syndicates at the expense of retail participants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What is at stake here is the credibility of our financial markets, something which should not be taken for granted.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But in this pursuit, we should also ensure that retail investors understand the complicated risks involved in the various classes of investment products and the penalties of misconduct.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, Madam, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Securities and Futures (Amendment) Bill introduces extensive changes and keeps standards in Singapore on par with international capital markets and best practices and ensures our capital markets regulatory framework keeps pace with market developments.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is important that we strengthen regulation of OTC derivatives markets in the wake of the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The proposed amendments are in line with the recommendations made by FSB and the G20.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Malpractice in the market can be very damaging.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Members of this House may recall when news broke of the extent of the LIBOR fixing in 2012, that scandal sent shock waves around the world.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As many as 20 big banks were named in various investigations or lawsuits alleging that LIBOR was rigged.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To many, the pervasive misconduct amongst traders felt like "daylight robbery", and served to further corrode what little remained of public trust in banks and those who run them.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore has not been immune to financial malpractice.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The revelation affected trust and confidence in Singapore's financial institutions.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There was widespread public outrage at the extent of bankers' misconduct, the flawed benchmark setting mechanisms that provided ample room for manipulation, and how the perpetrators got away with punishments that appeared light in comparison to the severity of their crimes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I therefore support the new regulatory framework proposed to instil better governance in the setting of financial benchmarks and transparency in the listed securities markets.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: My question to the Minister is whether the proposed enforcement regime is punitive enough to guard against capital market misconduct, to deter future offenders and to regain investor confidence.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Would the Minister also illustrate how the proposed criminal and civil penalties for capital market misconduct compare to those implemented in other international financial markets?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I urge the authorities to arm ourselves with a sufficiently "big stick" to weed out temptations to manipulate and use the full extent of the law to punish offenders.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many people wondered why it took so long to bring these products under MAS' oversight.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As the investment landscape evolves and the new "creative" financial instruments emerge to prey on unsuspecting investors, I urge the authorities to prioritise regulatory oversight in order to protect retail investors.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many consumers are particularly vulnerable in the current environment of low returns; they may be easily tempted by products that promise higher yields to make their hard-earned savings work harder.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Of course, individual investors must also protect themselves by doing their own homework, being responsible for their own investment decisions, and managing their financial assets in a manner appropriate to their stage in life.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In the world of investments, there is no free lunch.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Much more can be done to promote financial education in a systematic way, making financial literacy pervasive in our community and strengthening our immunity against mis-selling and fraud.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is especially key to helping our fast-ageing population preserve precious savings that provide the safety net they need in their retirement.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, this aim must be balanced with the equally important goal of keeping Singapore competitive as a world-class financial centre.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There is much concern in the industry about the overwhelming number and rate of regulatory changes taking place, just when the financial industry is facing significant headwinds of lower growth and squeezed margins.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Some players actually feel that their very survival is being threatened by escalating compliance costs as a result of the heavier regulatory burden.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There is a sense that jobs are being threatened, as are employment prospects of Singaporeans in this sector.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With this in mind, I am concerned about the timing to amend rules around AIs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst I agree with the intent of these proposed changes, which will enable high net worth individuals to benefit from the full range of safeguards for retail investors, I am worried about the capacity of banks to take action with yet another set of new regulations.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These include enhanced anti-money laundering measures as well as common reporting standards.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The changes proposed for the AI framework would involve private banks going through the extensive exercise of re-segmenting their business, reviewing every client account, with client calls to do more reviews.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For offshore clients, the exercise could prove challenging, given access to information on clients' liability is limited in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, I rise in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: First, let me talk about protecting our jobs in the financial industry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: These challenges have a direct and immediate impact on our people's job security.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As such, it is important that we keep both our regulations and the implementation of our regulations, flexible.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For a while after the Global Financial Crisis, there is a broad consensus on the regulatory direction.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, uncertainty in the direction has increased recently.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: After Brexit, it is unclear what the United Kingdom's (UK's) financial centre's role will be for the world and for the European Union.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Logically, UK regulations could change as her role evolves.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: After the US presidential election, it is unclear whether the Dobb-Frank Act still speaks for the future of US regulations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In short, as the trajectory of global regulations is increasingly unclear, we must be wise in the direction and pace of evolution of our own regulations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We must not front-run the regulations of the world's leading financial centres, or we will be holding our industry back from serving the needs of Asia and beyond.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As such, it would be helpful if MAS can provide a perspective on: Firstly, what is MAS' perspective on the evolution of US regulations, especially with regard to the Dobb-Frank Act?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: How do we see the UK's role as a financial centre and the UK's financial regulations evolve?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Does the UK's changing role represent opportunities or challenges for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: How do we factor in the conditions of emerging Asia, as well as the key markets that we serve, to ensure our industry stays competitive, so that we can protect our people's jobs?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, for the new framework on AIs, can MAS assure our industry that there will be adequate implementation safeguards to ensure that our industry, like what Ms Foo Mee Far has said, has room to adjust?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I would like to talk about promoting truth in lending and investing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The financial industry is both complex and competitive.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, lending cost is advertised differently for different products.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It is calculated differently for: (a) housing loans compared to car loans, (b) car loans compared to credit card loans; and (c) credit card loans compared to hire-purchase financing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Processing fees and penalty costs for these different products vary considerably, too.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Because of all these, consumers have difficulty understanding the true cost of their spending decisions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For decisions like buying a house or a vehicle, a miscalculation could be a big financial impact.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps, MAS can study international best practices, including from the US' "Truth in Lending" Act.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This Act requires the lenders to provide important pieces of information, such as the annual percentage rate (APR), the term of the loan, and the total cost for the borrowers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Would MAS also consider gradually aligning our companies towards communicating interest rates and lending cost, in a simple and unified way?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Related to truth in lending is transparency and straightforward information on other financial products, such as investments and insurance that the majority of Singaporeans use.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: By "majority", I refer to non-AIs, who may not have detailed financial information.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Compared to lending products, it is even harder to provide clarity on such products.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But I hope that MAS can push forward, even if complexity limits us to taking small steps.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Specifically, perhaps MAS can consider gradually getting our financial industry to adopt a common language, as well as a straightforward and concise approach, to explaining financial products.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We could, perhaps, pay more attention on how the industry explains: (a) returns; (b) price of product; (c) processing fees and penalties; (d) risks; and (e) duration of product coverage.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As I talk to many Singaporeans across differing age and income groups about financial security, a common theme emerges.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: (a) For the past few decades, many Singaporeans are assured of a steady career and income progression, as well as rising housing values.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: These provide both financial security and retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: (b) With the increasingly uncertain world, the financial cushion that Singaporeans are used to may not be there for all.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: (c) At the same time, while some Singaporeans are well-informed, wise and prudent in their financial decisions, some are not.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: (d) And good income or academic qualifications do not always equate to financial prudence or literacy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This will empower our people to be financially savvy and prudent in uncertain times.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If our schools are focused on preparing Singaporeans for the future, then teaching them how to guard and manage their finances is surely an important guarantee for their future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Two, during National Service, there are the occasional down time in between training.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to the response from MAS and I stand in full support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The proposed amendments to the Securities and Futures Act are an important step towards strengthening Singapore's position as a global financial centre and protecting our citizens' hard-earned savings.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I would, first, like to thank our colleagues at the Ministry of Finance for putting together numerous consultation papers which culminated in this very important Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This Bill builds on the amendment Bill of 2012.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At that time, I had spoken in support of the Ministry's move to impose a principles-based approach to the regulation of OTC derivatives.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Today, I would like to focus on measures to protect investors and, in particular, retail investors, like the many uncles and aunties who are just trying to have a comfortable retirement.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this low interest rate environment, they are trying their best to make their money work for them.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But they often lack the financial knowledge to determine if a product is right for them.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We still remember the heart-breaking stories of the many retirees who lost their entire life's savings during the Minibond debacle.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is, therefore, heartening to see that measures to enhance the regulatory safeguards for retail investors are a central component of the amendments.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Flip open the Straits Times today and you will see so many new, fangled investment schemes purporting high returns and low risk.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some deals seem too good to be true and, indeed, they are, or they are nothing but scams designed to separate the ordinary investor from his money.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I understand that risk is an inseparable part of the investment process, that higher returns necessarily involve higher risks.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We cannot and should not insulate investors from market risks because that is the natural order of things.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must, however, seek to protect them from fraudulent scams.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am concerned that the policeman is always chasing, but never catching, a shape-shifting thief.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The profit incentive strongly motivates financial innovation − new products, both good and bad, are being created all the time.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Backward-looking regulation can only prevent a recurrence of the previous crisis, but not to prevent the next one.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is telling that elements of this Bill, similar to many Bills around the world, are still reacting to the Global Financial Crisis of 2008, a full nine years ago.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What do we need to put in place to prevent the next crisis, the next scandal, and the next hit to the retirement finances of our loved ones?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In my humble opinion, a successful regulatory regime should have the following components.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One, eyes and ears: multiple channels that make it easy for the public to report suspicious activities, lodge complaints or become whistle-blowers.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Two, brains: a team of highly qualified experts who can quickly assess the risk profile and complexity of any new products, and flag potential risks.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Three, teeth: the power to act swiftly to blacklist or shut down any activity that is proven to be fraudulent or deemed to be highly dangerous.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And fourth, helping hands: tools that help retail investors make the right decisions.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Financial products can now be distributed through multiple channels, not all of them visible to the authorities.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To counter this, we should enlist the help of the public to flag any suspicious offerings.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The goal is to make this as simple and as painless as possible, to encourage people to highlight any products where malfeasance may be suspected.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While this may create false positives, it is more important here to avoid the converse problem of false negatives resulting in significant losses for investors.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Regulating new financial products is a challenging task.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On one side, you have some of the smartest people in the world who are so incentivised to create new products and very complicated products to make as much money as possible for themselves.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On the other hand, you have overburdened regulators trying to stay on top of new innovations over multiple asset classes.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One solution could be to create a committee that convenes to assess the complaints and determine if new structures and products are fraudulent.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This should be staffed by industry experts drawn from leading financial institutions, who would be called upon on a regular basis.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This means empowering them to make immediate and decisive action, including blacklisting or even shutting down entire asset classes.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It could also define which investor types are allowed to invest in a particular asset class.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Again, there might be "false positives" where the asset class ultimately proves to be legitimate, but the focus should be on protecting retail investors.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And if the expert panel judges that there is reason to believe that it is fraudulent, that it does not pass muster, then the committee puts it on a blacklist.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The committee acts as a "rapid response force" to flag suspicious activities, giving the regulators more time to respond to it fully.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Speed is of the essence here as we must stop fraudulent offerings before too many people get affected.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Ultimately, individual investors need to take responsibility for their own actions.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But given the asymmetry of information, they need help to decide.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The only challenge was that it required a high degree of technical expertise to execute well.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This would require additional regulatory resources, which I would like to encourage and support.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will start with answering some of the specific queries, followed by the broader considerations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Foo Mee Har asked about how our proposed criminal and civil penalties for capital market misconduct offences compare internationally and whether our penalties are sufficient to deter market misconduct and maintain investor confidence.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Louis Ng, too, asked if fines are a sufficient punishment and whether we should impose, say, a trading ban.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I agree with Ms Foo that the authorities should have a sufficiently big stick for deterrence.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS can pursue a wide range of enforcement actions, including penalties and criminal sanctions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The quantum of civil penalties that MAS can pursue and the maximum criminal imprisonment term for market misconduct offences are comparable with other major financial centres.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we all know that the key deterrent of any crime is the custodial sentence.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is comparable with the UK, also seven years; Hong Kong and Australia, 10 years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In addition, if the offender is a regulated person, MAS also has the powers to issue a prohibition order on him to ban him from the industry for a specified period of time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, what Mr Louis Ng has suggested can be done.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS can issue the prohibition order independently and separately from any criminal prosecution or civil penalty action proceedings.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is also important to remember that legally prescribed penalties are one side of the equation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To achieve a real deterrent effect, statutory penalties have to be complemented by swift and strong enforcement action.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That leads me to a point raised by Mr Leon Perera on the adequacy of resources in terms of enforcement.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And as the Member has noted in an earlier written reply, our resources are comparable to major regimes around the world.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Having said that, last year, in 2016, MAS set up a dedicated enforcement unit.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This will take on criminal powers of investigation and joint investigation of market misconduct offences, together with the Commercial Affairs Department.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It has also set up a civilian unit to monitor unusual trading activities, all with sufficient resources, including forensic and civilian analysts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Unfortunately, I would not be able to provide the Member with the exact number of officers because that should be confidential so that offenders do not start thinking and making calculations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the AI regime, I want to first assure Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Henry Kwek that our regime is also comparable internationally.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
