text: Specifically in relation to the thresholds for individuals based on their wealth, the thresholds in various regimes, excluding primary residence and expressed in Singapore dollars, are as follows: in the US, it is $1.4 million; the UK, $0.8 million; Hong Kong, $1.5 million.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi asked if we could use knowledge as a criterion for defining AI instead.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As he pointed out, investors who have more wealth may not necessarily be better informed or require less regulatory protection than retail investors.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Likewise, someone who has certain knowledge, such as having made certain investment transactions or worked in the financial industry for some time, also may not necessarily be sophisticated investors when it comes to their own money.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The truth is that all criteria are never perfect − we are all finding proxies and the best possible proxies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But the use of wealth or income thresholds, while not perfect, is a fairly objective proxy for financial sophistication and is also widely used by other regulators around the world.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: What is more pertinent is that now, we are introducing an opt-in regime.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With that, the specific AI-eligibility thresholds become much less critical.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In a similar vein, Mr Leon Perera asked several questions on what are the detailed calculations of the threshold.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To answer his question, it does include insurance and life policies; it does include all bonds, liquid or not.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But ultimately, because it is now an opt-in regime, the specifics of the thresholds are no longer so critical because the right is on the investor, whether you want to stay as a retail investor or you opt in to be accredited an AI.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To Mr Saktiandi's point on requiring third party certification of an investor's assets to assess AI-eligibility, financial institutions (FIs) currently must, and will continue to be expected to, conduct proper due diligence and maintain proper records of the basis of an investor's classification as an AI.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS supervises the FIs closely to ensure that they do so, but we do not prescribe the specific processes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi raised a fairly convoluted point that we allow all corporates or trusts to be AIs, so long as at least one shareholder or trust beneficiary is an AI, and similar to a flexibility which will be given to joint accounts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS has considered this carefully but we decided against it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The flexibility which will be given to joint accounts where at least one account holder is an AI is on the condition that every account holder opts in to be an AI, and only in respect of investment transactions made out of that joint account.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, unlike joint accounts, corporates and trusts are distinct legal persons, and shareholders and beneficiaries behind them do not enjoy that right to opt in.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hence, corporates and trusts should only be treated as AIs if they are AI-eligible in their own right, or all shareholders or beneficiaries are AIs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In response to industry's concerns − and this came about because of our consultation effort − the industry raised concerns on the potential impact to their business.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: FIs would only need to notify them of their right to opt out of the AI status, and the implications of their choices.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As what Ms Foo said, the industry should focus on providing better services and value to its customers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, this need not be at odds with the enhancements to the AI regime.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The new definition of AI is a sharper one and will accord protection to investors who need them the most.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The opt-in mechanism raises awareness of their own investment needs and a better understanding of the nature of their relationship with their financial service provider.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These are really the key reasons behind the changes to the AI scheme, a sharper protection, and is important for the long-term competitiveness of the industry and sophistication of the market.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I want to also assure Mr Thomas Chua that the proposed changes in this Bill will not affect crowdfunding of projects and startups.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In June last year, MAS had introduced measures to make it easier for startups to raise funds from investors through securities-based crowdfunding.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Foo Mee Har cautioned that new "creative" instruments will emerge to prey on unsuspecting investors.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon suggested setting up a committee to assess new structures or products that come onto the market.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I wish to highlight that there are existing channels through which MAS and other enforcement agencies receive information on such suspicious investments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These come from a wide range of sources, including members of the public, the financial industry and other regulatory and enforcement agencies, local as well as overseas.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Where information received suggests a breach of laws, the relevant experts within the authorities will investigate and take appropriate action.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It actually operates in similar ways as the committee suggested by Mr Ong Teng Koon.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But the function is operationally sited, as opposed to becoming a staffed committee.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To warn consumers early that they are dealing with entities that are not licensed by MAS, MAS publishes an Investors Alert List (IAL).

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The IAL contains a list of entities that may have been wrongly perceived by the public to be licensed by MAS.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Consumers are encouraged to exercise caution when dealing with such entities as they will not be able to rely on regulatory safeguards under SFA.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The list is not exhaustive and is updated based, in part, on public feedback and complaints received by MAS.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: What is different about Mr Ong Teng Koon's suggestion of a committee is a "guilty until proven innocent" approach.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, as highlighted by several Members of this House, this can be seen as draconian, and we must be mindful that an overly-regulated environment could stifle legitimate business and innovation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We should avoid inadvertently subjecting all forms of economic activities, involving consumers handing over monies to a third party in anticipation of a return, to financial regulation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We see them, such as in purchasing of wine or art; we do not want to inadvertently catch them all.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Also, in practice, the distinction between a legitimate product with a more speculative business model or strategy and a fraudulent one sometimes may not be that clear-cut.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A legitimate product, due to unexpected market conditions or turn of events, or even poor investment decisions, may not be able to deliver its claims.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Prejudging whether a new product is fraudulent is not straightforward.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Henry Kwek suggested improving disclosures for loans and investment products so that consumers can easily understand and compare the features.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Fees and charges are included in the calculation of EIRs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I agree that we can certainly do more to simplify and standardise disclosures for investment products.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As Mr Henry Kwek has rightly pointed out, the challenge is to do so in a way that adequately reflects the different investment risks and communicates the complex features, such as the payoffs under different scenarios and, yet, in a manner that investors can understand.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS has introduced guidelines for a Product Highlights Sheet (PHS) for offers of securities made with a prospectus.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: PHS is a simplified disclosure document that highlights salient features and risks of an investment product, including information on the type of investor that the product is suitable for, and fees and charges, in a clear and concise manner.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To encourage the industry to draft disclosures in a clear and comprehensive manner, MAS has also introduced guidelines on good drafting practices for prospectuses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Plain language is encouraged, and legal, financial or technical jargon that may not be easily understood by lay persons should be avoided.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi has suggested adopting the approach in Hong Kong, which requires FIs selling investment products to ensure the suitability of the products sold to investors.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: While we do not have this clause in Singapore, other similar safeguards are in place.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But the law can only go so far.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS expects FIs to deal with all investors fairly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The industry must do what is right, instead of focusing only on doing what is required under the law.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS will continue to work with the industry to improve such a culture.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As an international financial centre, we align our regulations to global standards or best practices where appropriate, but we will do so after careful consideration of our local market characteristics.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS will go above international standards where necessary or refrain from certain measures which we regard as less relevant in our context.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The implementation of OTC derivatives reform is actually a good example of how we balance such competing objectives.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We deliberately took a calibrated approach, in two phases, and for the first phase, focused on trade reporting and central clearing obligations because these have the biggest systemic implications.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Even for trade reporting, we did not take a "Big Bang" approach, but start with larger FIs, such as banks, and for larger asset classes, such as interest rate derivatives, first.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For clearing, it is a similar progressive implementation approach.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, Mr Henry Kwek is right to point out that we should monitor what is happening in the US and UK on the financial regulatory landscape.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It would be premature to say which direction regulatory evolution will go.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will be mindful that the regulatory pendulum does swing, and we do what is right, both as a key member of the international financial community and also ready for our local market.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The fact is that whatever reforms or policy reviews we do now, not just for financial services, in fact, for many other policy areas, we have to strike this judicious balance between safeguarding the interests of the public and encouraging innovation and dynamism.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And we must expect to hear different and sometimes opposing voices.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, just this Bill alone, Mr Saktiandi has suggested further tightening of the AI regime ‒ maybe raise the $2 million threshold.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Foo questioned, however, the need to implement this at this point in time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon asked for tighter regulations on non-conventional products and a "guilty until proven innocent" regime; Mr Thomas Chua, on the other hand, cautioned against stifling innovation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we hear this all the time and we have to strike that judicious balance.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Leon Perera also talked about this balance and smart regulations, and then went on to cite the example of President-Elect Trump's suggestion to ban the moving of civil servants into the financial industry.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We must, first, be clear that while the President-Elect has spoken about it, there has been no ban in the US on such movements.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you look at the key appointments of the Trump administration, several are, in fact, from the industry.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think Mr Leon Perera also asked if MAS imposes garden leave and cooling-off periods.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It ranges from three months to 12 months, depending on the seniority as well as the functional role of the officer.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But conflict of interests does exist and we all know that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ultimately, it is also an issue of integrity.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Given the reputation of MAS, the conduct of our officers and our track record, I do not think there is any suggestion that our system is currently inadequate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we will continue to do these ‒ impose a garden leave but allow a movement of talent from industry to Government, to any other sectors.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In that way, when we have regulation and policy reviews, there is greater understanding all round.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With integrity, this is a fundamental basis to prevent conflict of interests.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As Ms Foo Mee Har, Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Louis Ng have rightly pointed out, financial education efforts are, therefore, of utmost importance, and will be a key priority of MAS.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Through MoneySENSE, the national financial education programme, we have continued to step up on such efforts systematically.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MoneySENSE provides financial education to different segments of society, through mainstream media, public roadshows and seminars.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It also adopts a collaborative approach where the Government, financial industry and the wider community work together in outreach efforts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, MoneySENSE organises regular seminars on a wide range of investment and financial planning topics.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One popular series is the My Money Seminar which is organised with the Association of Banks in Singapore and the Securities Association of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These are for the general public and are conducted in both English and Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, MoneySENSE also has nation-wide educational campaigns that are conducted across multiple platforms, media channels and delivered in different languages to maximise outreach.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One example is the "I Save and Invest for Our Future" campaign last year, which encouraged Singaporeans to take a life-cycle approach to investing and highlighted the benefits of saving and investing from young.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The campaign also educated consumers on simple, low-cost investment products, such as the Singapore Savings Bonds and exchange-traded funds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Third, MoneySENSE also works closely with the Singapore Polytechnic's Institute for Financial Literacy (IFL) in developing and conducting free financial literacy talks and workshops delivered at the workplace and community level.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are also modules on investment-focused topics, such as "Fundamentals of Share Investing" and "Understanding Bonds".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Fourth, MoneySENSE recognises the need to better empower consumers to avoid falling prey to "get-rich-quick" schemes, and publishes consumer alerts on its website to warn consumers of unregulated products and schemes, and the key questions they should be asking as well as the red flags they should be looking out for when considering such investments or trading opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MoneySENSE and MAS also provide a number of resources on their websites, such as the MAS Financial Institutions Directory and the Investor Alert List.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, maintaining Singapore's reputation as a trusted and stable financial centre while ensuring ease of doing business and supporting financial sector innovation and growth.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, enhancing safeguards for investors while managing costs and impact of regulation on the financial industry and legitimate businesses.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Before we proceed, I propose to take the break now.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I think we sat for a long time.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair again at 5.10 pm.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.47 pm until 5.10 pm.
